decision.title: Cheap coercion of one item: single-item shortcuts (packet )
decision.summary: A matches and coerces one item against a plain atomic item type without the coercion engine, and the matcher's frames move out of its struct, cutting coercion costs.

item.p: Whom it serves: every function call with typed parameters, built-in or user-defined, above all XSLT that passes attribute values to string functions. A callgrind profile of SchXslt's expand stage of EN 16931 (75.3 x 10^9 instructions, 10.5 s, step bound raised in a scratch build) put 33 % in sxml_evaluator_coerce: 8.1 million coercions from COERCE leaves, about 3,000 instructions each. 4.8 million returned after a whole match (537 instructions a match, most of it making the matcher and its frames); 3.4 million ran the coercion engine, which made 4.1 million sequence builders, atomized 2.7 million nodes, cast 1.4 million xs:untypedAtomic values to xs:string and matched the value again before and after.
Mechanism (glossary ; src/evaluator_function.c), the one coercion and the one matcher, without new machinery:

Matching: sxml_evaluator_match_sequence_type decides no item by the occurrence and one item by the occurrence and the matcher's own item rules (sxml_type_matcher_advance_item), with no frames; whatever those rules do not decide at once (choices, typed maps, arrays and records, JNode value types) runs the matcher as before. One atomic item against xs:anyAtomicType matches at once (XPath 4.0, 3.2.3), as against its own annotation did ().

Coercion: one item against a plain atomic item type (variety atomic, not a union, choice or enumeration; not under the cast rules of 's composite casts) is coerced without the engine (3.4, 3.4.3): an instance of its type stays, before the type is read; else the item, or a node's typed value when it is one atomic item, goes through sxml_coerce_atomic_item once; an unchanged item needs no final match, a cast one still gets it. Atomized values of no item or several, and every other value and type, go to the engine from the beginning; atomizing again there raises what the first atomization would have.

The matcher's and the engine's four inline frames are an array of the caller's, not part of the struct, so making either writes no frames; the frame structs' fields are ordered for padding (clang-analyzer's optin.performance.Padding).

Not changed: outcomes, error codes (XPTY0004, the role's code, XPTY0117, FORG0001 and the XSLT roles' type errors of ), the order in which errors arise, and steps (coercion charges none; ). holds: no new loops over nested structure.

Measured (callgrind instructions x 10^9, release, before at e82b48d2e, after 44f8d546b): SchXslt expand 75.27 to 61.68 (-18 %), of which coercion 24.88 to 11.21 (about 1,380 instructions a coercion), the same output byte for byte; tests/bench/coercion.xq (new, in run-bench.py) 3.775 to 2.847 (-25 %); recursion.xq 5.268 to 5.114; xmark-all 8.737 to 8.735. By change, coercion.xq: matching and coercion shortcuts 3.775 to 3.190, frames out of the structs 2.999, xs:anyAtomicType 2.901, instances before the type is read 2.847 (recursion.xq had risen 0.8 % before that last step). Processor seconds (fastest of seven, a shared machine): coercion.xq 0.463 to 0.332, xmark-all 1.12 to 1.09; expand about 10.5 to 8.5. QT4 XP40 (32,785 passed), XQ40 (46,114) and XT40 (12,185), whole, release, case by case against the base commit built the same way: 0 outcomes differ.

Left: in the expand profile coercion is still 18 %: node atomization (3.1, the typed value's string), casts of xs:untypedAtomic to xs:string (2.2, about 1,600 instructions each through the cast pipeline: a relabelling of the same string would halve it, but belongs in src/cast.c), 0.7 million single items against unions, choices and enumerations still run the engine, and 0.7 million multi-item values run the whole matcher (some twice: a vector of 16 items or more whose slice base fails 's base match is matched again item by item). Multi-item values coerced to atomic types still match every item before, during and after the engine.
